messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

John, a fifty-two-year-old film director of European descent, has been navigating the aftermath of a life-altering event that continues to cast long shadows over his daily life. Married and part of a close-knit community in Los Angeles, John's world was upended two years ago when he survived a near-fatal car accident on one of his frequent trips between sets. John recalls the day vividly: the screeching tires, the blinding flash of headlights, and then silence. After waking up in the hospital with multiple fractures and a severe concussion, John thought he had dodged fate’s bullet. However, over time, he began to realize that this accident was not just a physical ordeal but an emotional one as well. In his role as a film director, John often works long hours on set, juggling complex scripts and coordinating large crews. Yet, since the accident, he finds himself increasingly distracted and irritable, unable to focus on details or manage tasks with the same ease that once came naturally. His anxiety is palpable; whenever a siren wails in the distance or an ambulance passes by, John’s heart races and his palms grow clammy. These moments often trigger intrusive memories of the accident, leaving him feeling disoriented and detached from reality. John's wife has noticed changes as well. He has become more distant and withdrawn, finding it difficult to engage in conversations that don’t revolve around work. On weekends, when he used to enjoy hiking with his family or attending film festivals, John now prefers staying home, often spending hours staring out the window or pacing back and forth across their living room. One of the most distressing aspects for John is the recurring nightmares that have become a nightly occurrence. In these dreams, he relives the moment of impact, feeling the bone-jarring jolt as his car was struck. He awakens in cold sweats, often gasping for breath, and finds it hard to fall back asleep due to the lingering sense of fear and vulnerability. Even when not dreaming, John experiences hypervigilance, always on edge and scanning his environment for potential threats. This hyper-awareness makes everyday activities like driving or even crossing a street a source of significant anxiety. He avoids highways altogether, preferring local roads where he feels more in control, though this often means longer commutes to set. John’s creative process has also been affected by the trauma. Scenes that once came easily now seem fraught with tension and hesitation. Recently, while filming a car chase sequence for an action movie, John found himself unable to direct the stunt team without feeling his own pulse quicken and his hands trembling. The memories of the accident were too close to home, and he felt acutely aware of how fragile life can be. Despite these challenges, John remains committed to his craft. He continues to work on projects that inspire him but finds himself constantly grappling with internal turmoil. His relationships have also suffered; friends comment on how much quieter he has become, and even at home, conversations often turn into awkward silences as he retreats inward. John’s wife tries to support him, offering a listening ear or suggesting they see a therapist together. However, John struggles with the idea of opening up about his fears and insecurities. The stigma around mental health is still present for him, making it difficult to seek help even when he knows it might be beneficial. As days turn into months, John’s coping mechanisms have shifted from denial to acceptance, albeit reluctantly. He acknowledges that something needs to change but struggles with how to move forward. Despite the lingering trauma, John continues to push through each day, holding onto hope that things will eventually improve and life can return to a semblance of normalcy. His journey is marked by resilience and determination, as he grapples with the specter of his near-fatal accident while striving to reclaim his sense of self and purpose in the world.
